title: Fort Shinnecock
summary: Fort Shinnecock marks a Shinnecock Hills landscape associated with a contact-period Shinnecock fort tradition and with June Meeting, a Native Christian gathering connected to Reverend John Cuffee and Eastern Long Island Native communities. Development has disrupted much of the historic landscape, so interpretation should remain careful, broad, and respectful.
map_geometry_source: Broad public orientation point for Shinnecock Hills from OSM/Nominatim and Directus text; not the sacred erratic, fort, or preserved area.
why_this_matters: A sacred glacial erratic in the Shinnecock Hills marks the suspected site of an contact-period fort and the historic gathering grounds for the annual June Meeting. Recognizing these enduring communal spaces highlights how the Shinnecock people creatively blended traditional Algonquian harvest ceremonies with new religious practices to sustain their tribal bonds through centuries of profound cultural change.
oral_history_content: According to Shinnecock oral history, this famous painting of David Pharoah depicts his journey towards one of the western council rocks. This painting is by E.L. Henry titled "Beach Wagon" 1880. Labeled "The King of the Montauks" in The Long Island Forum of May, 1944. For many years a photograph of the painting, labeled "Jerry Wright," also a Montauk and thought to be a contemporary of David Pharoah, hung in the East Hampton Free Library. A pastel version is featured on Gaynell Stone's book The History & Archaeology of the Montauk Vol 3. 1
history_content:
1990 Fort Shinnecock newspaper source

A 1990 newspaper article titled 1,000 Year Old Indian Fort Found reported on archaeological evidence in the Shinnecock Hills and the development pressure around the fort-area landscape.

Source: Dans Papers, 1990, project archive / Shinnecock Archaeology and History Drive folder.
colonial_description_content:
June Meeting in older sources

Nathaniel S. Prime and later local writers described June Meeting through nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century outsider language. Some of that language used terms such as "remnants," racial categories, and "outdated descriptions of custom." Those words reflect colonial and racial assumptions, not the meaning of June Meeting to Shinnecock, Unkechaug, Montaukett, and related Native Christian communities.

June Meeting is better understood as a continuing gathering shaped by worship, kinship, visiting, food, memory, and community renewal. Older descriptions can still help document the event's public visibility, but they reflect outside interpretation and should not be repeated as neutral descriptions of Native identity or religion.

Source context: Nathaniel S. Prime, A History of Long Island From Its First Settlement, 1845, p. 118; Harry D. Sleight, Historical Long Island, 1928.
